conditions: x is finite real, angles are in radians, and sqrt denotes the nonnegative real square root. Determine the complete real domain of the original integrand independently of the integration interval.
Evaluate the definite integral over the full closed interval [0,2*pi]. Require an explicit exact value; an unevaluated integral or numerical approximation is not acceptable.
Include points where the radicand is zero. A square root of a real square must be treated as an absolute value unless its sign has been established on the relevant interval.

properties: The complete original real domain is R: 0<=1+sin(x)<=2 everywhere. The integrand is continuous and has period 2*pi.
Its zeros are exactly x=3*pi/2+2*k*pi for integers k. In [0,2*pi] the only zero is 3*pi/2; it is included and creates no improper-integral singularity.
Both endpoints are regular points with integrand value 1. The exact integral is 4*sqrt(2).

The globally valid identity is sqrt(1+sin(x))=sqrt(2)*abs(cos(x/2-pi/4)). In the integration interval the cosine changes sign at x=3*pi/2, so dropping its absolute value across the entire interval gives an incorrect result.

cases.reason: For every real x, sine exists and lies in [-1,1], so its shifted value 1+sin(x) is nonnegative. This is precisely the necessary and sufficient condition for the specified real square root, proving that every real x is allowed, including all radicand zeros. Continuity of sine and the nonnegative square root proves continuity of the integrand, hence ordinary Riemann integrability on [0,2*pi]. The zeros follow from sin(x)=-1, and substitution gives value 1 at both endpoints. The half-angle identity gives 1+sin(x)=2*cos(x/2-pi/4)^2, so the nonnegative square root is sqrt(2)*abs(cos(x/2-pi/4)) globally. Put t=x/2-pi/4; then dx=2*dt and the bounds become -pi/4 and 3*pi/4. Cosine is nonnegative on [-pi/4,pi/2] and nonpositive on [pi/2,3*pi/4]. Therefore the integral is 2*sqrt(2)*([sin(t)] from -pi/4 to pi/2 - [sin(t)] from pi/2 to 3*pi/4)=2*sqrt(2)*((1+sqrt(2)/2)+(1-sqrt(2)/2))=4*sqrt(2). Splitting at the included zero is justified by continuity, and every transformation preserves the specified nonnegative root. Periodicity follows directly from sin(x+2*pi)=sin(x).
